paragraphs.context: In older ED patients with suspected delirium, there is sufficient direct evidence to select delirium diagnostic instruments that accurately rule in (i.e., confirm) or rule out (i.e., exclude) delirium [ 22 ]. The 4AT had the largest quantity of ED‐based research and may be used to rule in or rule out delirium [ 90 ]. The CAM‐ICU, brief Confusion Assessment Method (bCAM), modified Confusion Assessment Method (mCAM) for the Emergency Department, AMT‐4, and Richmond Agitation and Sedation Scale (RASS) are superior to clinical gestalt [ 91 ], and may also be used to rule in or rule out delirium. The Delirium Triage Screen is superior to clinical gestalt in ruling out delirium [ 92 ] (Table 3 ).
paragraphs.highlight: rule out (i.e., exclude) delirium
paragraphs.note: 'Rule out' refers to excluding the delirium diagnosis with a screening instrument (a diagnostic action), not the hand-off item of listing which alternative causes were excluded.

paragraphs.context: Delirium may be associated with many disease processes or medication interactions, including neurological etiologies such as stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, and brain tumors [ 131 ]. Often, the etiology for delirium is undifferentiated in the ED. Obtaining a head CT is common practice in older adults presenting to the ED with altered mental status (AMS), occurring in 13%–23% [ 132 , 133 ]. No clear guidance exists on whether to obtain a head CT in older adults presenting to the ED with delirium. The American College of Radiology (ACR) Appropriateness Criteria recommend obtaining brain imaging (specifically, a non‐contrast head CT) in patients with AMS, coma, delirium, or acute psychosis “unless the etiology is clear and the risk of intracranial pathology is low” [ 134 ].
paragraphs.highlight: the etiology for delirium is undifferentiated in the ED
paragraphs.note: Nearest match on 'cause/etiology,' but framed as whether to obtain a head CT to find an etiology (an imaging-workup decision), not communicating the suspected cause at hand-off.

paragraphs.context: RHealthcare professionals should follow established pathways of good care to manage patients with delirium. First consider acute, life-threatening causes of delirium, including low oxygen level, low blood pressure, low glucose level, and drug intoxication or withdrawal. Systematically identify and treat potential causes (medications, acute illness, etc), noting that multiple causes are common. Optimise physiology, management of concurrent conditions, environment (reduce noise), medications, and natural sleep, to promote brain recovery. Specifically detect, assess causes of, and treat agitation and/or distress, using nonpharmacological means only if possible (see section 7 for pharmacological treatment). Communicate the diagnosis to patients and carers, encourage involvement of carers and provide ongoing engagement and support. Aim to prevent complications of delirium such as immobility, falls, pressure sores, dehydration, malnourishment, isolation. Monitor for recovery and consider specialist referral if not recovering. Consider follow up (see section 8).
paragraphs.highlight: Systematically identify and treat potential causes (medications, acute illness, etc), noting that multiple causes are common
paragraphs.note: Supports both hand-off components — first rule out acute life-threatening causes, then systematically identify the (often multiple) underlying causes.

paragraphs.context: Once delirium is diagnosed in the ED, the diagnostic evaluation should then focus on uncovering the underlying etiology.48 Infections, such as a urinary tract infection or pneumonia, dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, central nervous system insults, and medication reactions are common causes.32 If admitted, physicians at the next level of care should be notified of the patient's delirium status. Other than these interventions, however, the optimal management of delirium is still unclear, especially within the ED setting. Several multi-component delirium interventions have been developed for hospitalized patients and can be tailored for the ED,49, 50 but their efficacy is questionable.51 Because many of these interventions were started 24 to 48 hours after admission, early detection and early intervention of delirium in the ED may improve their effectiveness similar to what has been observed in sepsis and ST-elevation myocardial infarction care.52, 53 A multi-faceted line of research must be undertaken to develop delirium interventions specifically tailored for the ED setting and determine their cost-effectiveness using randomized control trial methodology.

claims.synthesis: The on-scope sources agree: the primary anchor ADEPT (2020, p.7) directs the ED team to explicitly communicate the delirium diagnosis to the receiving team and to identify/rule out its underlying cause, and Han 2010, SIGN 157, and NICE CG103 concur that the etiology should be worked up and the delirium diagnosis documented/notified at transfer of care — together governing the "suspected cause(s) and what was ruled out" hand-off item. The nearest-match content in GED Guidelines 2.0, Han 2013, and the 4AT is different-scope (diagnostic "rule out delirium" screening and head-CT etiology workup): it shares keywords but must not be read as direct support, and ADEPT p.7 governs as the primary ED hand-off source.

claims.passage:
… In addition, it is important that the ED clinicians and nursing staff communicate the presence of delirium or agitation to the inpatient team. When the diagnosis of delirium is not made in the ED, it is also more likely to be missed by the inpatient teams,1 so it is important that the diagnosis be communicated explicitly. TREAT The fifth is "Treat." The overall goal for treatment of delirium in the ED is to identify and address the underlying cause while avoiding actions or inactions that may worsen delirium. Following the preventive steps outlined in this review will assist with these goals. paragraphs.context: In addition to the dramatic effect that these instruments could have on the routine clinical practice, the availability of feasible assessments will open a new frontier to additional delirium investigations. As with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction and severe sepsis care, we envision establishing similar paradigms for delirium care in which early identification and intervention in the ED of delirious patients at higher risk is emphasized.43, 44 However, a multi-faceted investigative approach must be taken to achieve this goal. We must determine if our two-step approach captures patients at highest risk for adverse outcomes and those who would benefit most from intervention. Several delirium multi-component interventions exist for hospitalized patients, but their efficacy has been equivocal.45 Many of these studies, however, enrolled delirious patients across the entire spectrum of severity 24 to 48 hours after admission. Conceivably, performing these interventions in high-risk delirious patients early in the ED course may cost-effectively improve short- and long-term outcomes. This hypothesis should be tested in future investigations using randomized-control trial methodology.

paragraphs.context: Once delirium is diagnosed in the ED, the diagnostic evaluation should then focus on uncovering the underlying etiology.48 Infections, such as a urinary tract infection or pneumonia, dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, central nervous system insults, and medication reactions are common causes.32 If admitted, physicians at the next level of care should be notified of the patient's delirium status. Other than these interventions, however, the optimal management of delirium is still unclear, especially within the ED setting. Several multi-component delirium interventions have been developed for hospitalized patients and can be tailored for the ED,49, 50 but their efficacy is questionable.51 Because many of these interventions were started 24 to 48 hours after admission, early detection and early intervention of delirium in the ED may improve their effectiveness similar to what has been observed in sepsis and ST-elevation myocardial infarction care.52, 53 A multi-faceted line of research must be undertaken to develop delirium interventions specifically tailored for the ED setting and determine their cost-effectiveness using randomized control trial methodology.

paragraphs.context: performed the RASS using the same sequence of 3 steps as outlined in Table 1. If the patients were alert or agitated prior to stimulation, they were scored 0 to+4 accordingly. If patients were not spontaneously alert, they were then called by name to look at the rater, with the duration of eye contact measured, at which time a positive response was scored accordingly as -1 to -3. If the patients did not respond to verbal stimulation, they were then physically stimulated (ie, shoulder shake and/or sternal rub) and scored according to their response as -4 or -5. If calm and not alert prior to verbal and physical stimulation, patients were then rated as -1 to -5 (as standardized in Table 1) even if they became agitated on stimulation. Assessments required less than 20 seconds.

paragraphs.context: Background Disorientation is an early indicator of developing postoperative delirium (POD), which is associated with increased mortality and cognitive decline. The well-established "Confusion-Assessment-Method-for-IntensiveCare-Unit" (CAM-ICU) for diagnosing POD in intubated patients cannot make use of the feature `disorientation', as this requires verbal communication. Other tools such as the 4AT test for disorientation but are not established in ICU settings. We therefore combined test-variables of the CAM-ICU (level of consciousness, fluctuating mental status and inattention) with verbal testing for disorientation to develop and enhance diagnostic accuracy of the "Confusion Assessment Method for Intermediate Care Unit" (CAM-IMC). In the present study we describe the development and the evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy of the CAM-IMC.
paragraphs.highlight: test-variables of the CAM-ICU (level of consciousness, fluctuating mental status and inattention)
paragraphs.note: Level of consciousness is one of the CAM-IMC's constituent test-variables, directly supporting 'It is the CAM-IMC's level-of-consciousness item.'

paragraphs.context: The elements “Acute change or fluctuating course of mental status” and “Altered level of consciousness” are dichotomous, allowing for the assignment of one point for an abnormal test result.
paragraphs.highlight: “Altered level of consciousness” are dichotomous, allowing for the assignment of one point for an abnormal test result
paragraphs.note: The CAM-IMC's point-based scoring names 'Altered level of consciousness' as a dichotomous element scoring one point for an abnormal result — the tool's level-of-consciousness item.

paragraphs.context: By creating the CAM-IMC flowchart design as a pointbased scoring system, the importance of disorientation as a central feature of POD has been reinforced. The features disorientation and inattention can each trigger a positive test result. The system assigns up to five points for disorientation and three points for inattention, thereby increasing the weight of these single features in the overall diagnosis. The categories of acute or fluctuating change and RASS0 have been reduced in significance and each contribute one point to the total score but are not mandatory for a positive test outcome. This is reflected in their limited ability to discriminate POD, as shown by a distinct lower AUROC compared to disorientation, inattention and overall CAM-IMC. As a result, disorientation and inattention exert the greatest influence Beyer et al.
paragraphs.highlight: each contribute one point to the total score but are not mandatory for a positive test outcome
paragraphs.note: The level-of-consciousness element is operationalized via RASS (RASS other than 0), confirming arousal/RASS is the CAM-IMC's LOC item; note it contributes one point and is not the gating step.

claims.synthesis: The statement's two clauses are supported by different on-scope sources: the RASS administration sequence (score arousal first, observe-then-verbal-then-physical = Look/Talk/Touch) is defined by Sessler 2002 and validated by Ely 2003, while 'altered level of consciousness' is confirmed as a CAM-IMC element operationalized by RASS in Beyer 2024, whose non-intubated intermediate-care setting matches the step-down card. paragraphs.context: The RASS is an arousal scale commonly used in intensive care units to assess for depth of sedation (Figure 1),10 but has been incorporated into several delirium assessments to assess for level of consciousness.6 For this study, we replaced the term "sedation" with "drowsy," (Figure 1) to describe level of consciousness regardless of sedation administration. A RASS of 0 represented normal level of consciousness whereas a RASS other than 0 represented the presence of altered level of consciousness. The RASS was determined by an emergency physician (EP) and research assistants (RAs; college graduates, emergency medical technicians, and paramedics). Before the study began, the RAs were given a 5-minute didactic lecture about the RASS. The principal investigator then observed them perform the RASS in five older ED patients and provided them instruction if there was any discordance.

paragraphs.context: Conclusions--In older ED patients, a RASS other than 0 has very good sensitivity and specificity for delirium as diagnosed by a psychiatrist. A RASS > +1 or < -1 is nearly diagnostic for delirium given the very high positive likelihood ratio.

Han 2015 supplies the same RASS-not-0 = altered-arousal operational definition but validates it as a standalone delirium screen in older ED patients — a different setting and use — so it grounds the definition without addressing the CAM-IMC +1 scoring.

claims.statement: RASS −4 / −5 → STOP — stupor or coma; the CAM-IMC cannot be scored now. Reassess when the patient responds to voice.
claims.passage:
for diagnosing POD in intubated patients cannot make use of the feature ‘disorientation’, as this requires verbal communication. Other tools such as the 4AT test for disorientation but are not established in ICU settings.
Also Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC) (p. 3): “Inattention was assessed by having the patient read aloud a ten-letter word (ANANASBAUM or CASABLANCA) and squeeze the examiner’s hand each time they heard the letter “A.””
Also Han 2015 (RASS in the ED) (p. 3): “Patients were excluded if they were non-English speaking, deaf or blind, previously enrolled, non-verbal or unable to follow simple commands prior to their acute illnesses, comatose, or did not complete all the study assessments.”

The CAM-IMC's disorientation and inattention items require the patient to speak and follow commands (read a word aloud, squeeze the hand), so a patient who does not respond to voice cannot complete them (Beyer 2024, p. 1, p. 3); Han 2015 excluded comatose / non-verbal patients from RASS-based delirium assessment for the same reason (p. 3). The specific −4 / −5 cut-off and 'reassess when the patient responds to voice' are standard CAM-ICU / RASS practice (RASS −4 = no response to voice, −5 = unarousable; Sessler 2002, not archived), not wording quoted from the cited step-down sources.

paragraphs.context: This cohort study evaluates the test performance of the newly developed CAM-IMC and its disorientation component in a prospective cohort study. The CAM-IMC shows a sensitivity of 0.96 and specificity of 0.94 in diagnosis of POD in non-intubated postoperative cardiac surgery patients. Its test performance is comparable to the widely used CAM-ICU demonstrating a high level of accuracy [ 19 ]. While testing for disorientation alone shows good test performance values, it does not surpass the CAM-IMC. The study indicates that using the CAM-IMC by combing the features of the CAM-ICU with assessing of disorientation as a verbal testing variable, improves effectiveness and provides excellent sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing POD. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating verbal testing for disorientation whenever patients are accessible to oral evaluation to improve POD diagnostics. The CAM-IMC outperforms each individual feature of the CAM-IMC.
paragraphs.highlight: whenever patients are accessible to oral evaluation
paragraphs.note: The CAM-IMC's disorientation testing can only be applied when the patient is accessible to oral evaluation, which is exactly why a stuporous/comatose patient (RASS -4/-5) cannot be scored.

paragraphs.context: Background Disorientation is an early indicator of developing postoperative delirium (POD), which is associated with increased mortality and cognitive decline. The well-established "Confusion-Assessment-Method-for-IntensiveCare-Unit" (CAM-ICU) for diagnosing POD in intubated patients cannot make use of the feature `disorientation', as this requires verbal communication. Other tools such as the 4AT test for disorientation but are not established in ICU settings. We therefore combined test-variables of the CAM-ICU (level of consciousness, fluctuating mental status and inattention) with verbal testing for disorientation to develop and enhance diagnostic accuracy of the "Confusion Assessment Method for Intermediate Care Unit" (CAM-IMC). In the present study we describe the development and the evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy of the CAM-IMC.
paragraphs.highlight: with verbal testing for disorientation
paragraphs.note: The CAM-IMC (the tool the card cites) adds verbal testing for disorientation to the CAM-ICU features, so it requires a patient who can respond verbally; matches the primary anchor at p.1.

paragraphs.context: RASS ranges from -5 (deeply sedated) to +4 (aggressive)
paragraphs.highlight: -5 (deeply sedated)
paragraphs.note: Table 1 footnote defining the deep-sedation pole of the RASS (-5 = deeply sedated), anchoring the coma/deeply-sedated end of the STOP gate.

paragraphs.context: The Confusion-Assessment-Method for Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU), which originally derived from the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), was developed for monitoring of POD in intubated ICU-patients [ 19 , 20 ]. It omits the feature ‘disorientation’, as this requires a more differentiated verbal response than ‘yes’ and ‘no’, or nodding ‘yes’ and shaking your head ‘no’. Disorientation should not be missed as a frequent symptom and early indicator of POD as stated above. Screening for disorientation has been shown to provide high sensitivity (96.6%) in the diagnosis of POD [ 21 ].
paragraphs.highlight: was developed for monitoring of POD in intubated ICU-patients
paragraphs.note: Nearest match on the same arousal/level-of-consciousness theme but describes the CAM-ICU for intubated ICU patients — a different tool and population; the card uses the non-intubated CAM-IMC, which inherits the same arousal-gate logic.

paragraphs.context: because the psychiatrists' comprehensive assessments were conducted in addition to their clinical duties. The first patient who met all the eligibility criteria was enrolled each day. Patients who were 65 years or older, in the ED for less than 12 hours at the time of enrollment, and not in a hallway bed were eligible. The 12 hour cut-off was used to include patients who presented to the ED in the evening and early morning hours. Patients were excluded if they were non-English speaking, deaf or blind, previously enrolled, non-verbal or unable to follow simple commands prior to their acute illnesses, comatose, or did not complete all the study assessments. Patients who were non-verbal or unable to follow simple commands prior to their acute illnesses were considered to have end-stage dementia. These patients were excluded because diagnosing delirium in this patient group can be challenging, even for an experienced psychiatrist.
paragraphs.highlight: comatose, or did not complete all the study assessments
paragraphs.note: Comatose patients were excluded from this ED validation because delirium cannot be assessed in them — parallels the gate concept but is an ED enrollment exclusion, not an IMC/CAM-IMC arousal gate.

paragraphs.context: The RASS is an arousal scale commonly used in intensive care units to assess for depth of sedation (Figure 1),10 but has been incorporated into several delirium assessments to assess for level of consciousness.6 For this study, we replaced the term "sedation" with "drowsy," (Figure 1) to describe level of consciousness regardless of sedation administration. A RASS of 0 represented normal level of consciousness whereas a RASS other than 0 represented the presence of altered level of consciousness. The RASS was determined by an emergency physician (EP) and research assistants (RAs; college graduates, emergency medical technicians, and paramedics). Before the study began, the RAs were given a 5-minute didactic lecture about the RASS. The principal investigator then observed them perform the RASS in five older ED patients and provided them instruction if there was any discordance.
paragraphs.highlight: but has been incorporated into several delirium assessments to assess for level of consciousness
paragraphs.note: General framing of the RASS as an arousal / level-of-consciousness scale — background to why the RASS defines the gate's arousal thresholds.

paragraphs.context: Delirium is an under-recognized public health problem that is frequently missed by ED health care providers because it is not routinely screened for. The RASS may be a reasonable alternative to screen for delirium in the fast-paced ED environment. Because the RASS can be performed with a brief structured observation, it can be easily incorporated into the routine ED clinical work flow. We observed that a RASS other than 0 had very good sensitivity and specificity and moderately affected the likelihood of delirium. A RASS > +1 or < -1 was nearly diagnostic of delirium as evidenced by its very high specificity and likelihood ratio; no further delirium assessments would be needed in these patients. Despite a brief training period, there was moderately good agreement between the research staff and physician.
paragraphs.highlight: a RASS other than 0 had very good sensitivity and specificity
paragraphs.note: Han used the RASS itself as a delirium detector (RASS other than 0 = likely delirium) in older ED patients — a different use of the RASS than the arousal STOP-gate in this claim.

claims.synthesis: The on-scope governing source is Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC): it establishes the CAM-IMC as a verbal delirium test for non-intubated step-down patients that can only be applied when the patient is accessible to oral evaluation, which directly supports stopping and not scoring at RASS -4/-5 (stupor/coma), while the specific RASS thresholds and the 'responds to voice' reassessment trigger come from the Sessler 2002 scale definition. Han 2015 is the nearest match on RASS and arousal but is an ED study that used the RASS as a delirium screen and explicitly excluded comatose patients, so it is a different setting and a different use of the RASS and does not govern this arousal gate.

claims.statement: CAM-IMC positive = total ≥ 3 of 10.
claims.passage:
Patients scoring three points or higher were considered as positive for POD, while those less than three points were considered negative.
Also Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC) (p. 5): “The system assigns up to five points for disorientation and three points for inattention, thereby increasing the weight of these single features in the overall diagnosis. The categories of acute or fluctuating change and RASS≠0 have been reduced in significance and each contribute one point to the total score”
Exact match. Beyer 2024 set the CAM-IMC cut-off at three points by the Youden index — patients scoring ≥ 3 are positive, < 3 negative (p. 4). The maximum is 10: disorientation up to 5 + inattention up to 3 + acute change 1 + altered LOC 1 (p. 5).
citations: Beyer LP, et al. Disorientation as a delirium feature in non-intubated patients: development and evaluation of the CAM-IMC. BMC Anesthesiol 2024;24:451.

claims.statement: Acute change or fluctuating course (+1). Prompt: “Acute change from the patient’s mental-status baseline, or fluctuation over the past 24 h?”
claims.passage:
The elements “Acute change or fluctuating course of mental status” and “Altered level of consciousness” are dichotomous, allowing for the assignment of one point for an abnormal test result.
Supported. Acute change / fluctuating course is one of the two dichotomous CAM-IMC elements, scoring one point when abnormal (Beyer 2024, p. 3). The 24-hour / baseline framing restates the CAM/CAM-ICU acute-change feature the CAM-IMC inherits.
citations: Beyer LP, et al. Disorientation as a delirium feature in non-intubated patients: development and evaluation of the CAM-IMC. BMC Anesthesiol 2024;24:451.

The elements “Acute change or fluctuating course of mental status” and “Altered level of consciousness” are dichotomous, allowing for the assignment of one point for an abnormal test result.
Also Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC) (p. 8): “RASS ≠ 0 and disorientation are binary”

claims.statement: Inattention (0–3). Script: “Read the 10-letter word ‘ANANASBAUM’ (or ‘CASABLANCA’) aloud, letter by letter, and squeeze my hand each time you hear the letter A.” One point per error, to a maximum of 3; the item alone is positive at ≥ 3 errors.
claims.passage:
Inattention was assessed by having the patient read aloud a ten-letter word (ANANASBAUM or CASABLANCA) and squeeze the examiner’s hand each time they heard the letter “A.” Consistent with the CAM-ICU, a maximum of three errors were permitted, with one point deducted for each mistake.
Also Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC) (p. 8): “Cut-Off for ANANASBAUM-test was three or more errors. Cut-Off for Disorientation was two or more errors.”
Exact match. The read-aloud script (ten-letter word ANANASBAUM or CASABLANCA, squeeze on the letter A), the one-point-per-error scoring to a maximum of 3, and the item-level positive at ≥ 3 errors are all Beyer 2024 (p. 3; cut-off note p. 8).
citations: Beyer LP, et al. Disorientation as a delirium feature in non-intubated patients: development and evaluation of the CAM-IMC. BMC Anesthesiol 2024;24:451.

claims.statement: Disorientation (0–5): Age, Date of birth, Place, Year, Situational awareness. One point per error across five dimensions; the item alone is positive at ≥ 2 errors.
claims.passage:
we chose the four dimensions age, date of birth, place and year
Also Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC) (p. 4): “The fifth dimension we added was ‘situational awareness’”
Also Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC) (p. 4): “Each error in these dimensions resulted in one point, with a maximum of five points possible.”
Also Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC) (p. 8): “Cut-Off for ANANASBAUM-test was three or more errors. Cut-Off for Disorientation was two or more errors.”
Exact match. Beyer 2024 evaluates disorientation across five dimensions — age, date of birth, place, year, and the newly added situational awareness — one point per error to a maximum of 5 (p. 4), with the item positive at ≥ 2 errors (cut-off note, p. 8). The card's five dimensions match verbatim.
citations: Beyer LP, et al. Disorientation as a delirium feature in non-intubated patients: development and evaluation of the CAM-IMC. BMC Anesthesiol 2024;24:451.

claims.statement: For the verbal, non-intubated patient. Disorientation or inattention can drive a positive on their own.
claims.passage:
The features disorientation and inattention can each trigger a positive test result.
Also Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC) (p. 6): “the CAM-ICU does not diagnose POD if “Acute change or fluctuating course of the mental status” is assessed as negative, even when inattention or disorganized thinking” is present. By employing a point-based scoring system, the CAM-IMC avoids this limitation.”
Also Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC) (p. 5): “The CAM-IMC shows a sensitivity of 0.96 and specificity of 0.94 in diagnosis of POD in non-intubated postoperative cardiac surgery patients.”
Supported. Beyer 2024 states disorientation and inattention can each trigger a positive result and — unlike the CAM-ICU, which requires a positive acute-change feature — the CAM-IMC's point system removes that veto (p. 5–6). The CAM-IMC was validated in non-intubated post-cardiac-surgery intermediate-care patients (sensitivity 0.96 / specificity 0.94; p. 5); applying it across the broader step-down / progressive-care population is a reasonable but noted scope extension.
citations: Beyer LP, et al. Disorientation as a delirium feature in non-intubated patients: development and evaluation of the CAM-IMC. BMC Anesthesiol 2024;24:451.

claims.statement: Admission delirium risk (Martinez): three admission variables, 0–3 points, banded to predicted incidence. A validated ward prediction rule for direct admits — use it to target the prevention bundle.
claims.passage:
the individual risk of delirium is obtained by adding one point for each criterion met (age≥85, high level of dependence, and being on psychotropic medication).
Also Martinez 2012 (ward risk rule) (p. 4): “One point was given to patients older than 85 years, to those who had two or more points in the variable drugs, and to those with impairments in ﬁve or more of the ADL”
Supported. Martinez 2012 derived and validated a medical-ward rule adding one point each for age ≥ 85, dependence in ≥ 5 of 6 ADLs, and a psychotropic-drug subtotal ≥ 2 (abstract; p. 4). Using the score to target prevention aligns with NICE CG103's risk-factor-based prevention approach.

paragraphs.context: prediction rule, based on variables easily measurable at admission, to identify patients at high risk of developing delirium during their hospital stay on an internal medicine ward.
paragraphs.highlight: to identify patients at high risk of developing delirium during their hospital stay on an internal medicine ward
paragraphs.note: States the aim — derive and validate an admission-measurable prediction rule for internal-medicine ward inpatients, matching the claim's validated ward rule for direct admits.

paragraphs.context: analysed and finally included in the rule were: being aged 85 years old or older, being dependent in five or more activities of daily living, and taking two or more psychotropic drugs (antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, antidepressants, anticonvulsant and/or antidementia drugs). The variable of interest was delirium as defined by the short Confusion Assessment Method, which assesses four characteristics: acute onset and fluctuating course, inattention, disorganised thinking and altered level of consciousness.
paragraphs.highlight: being aged 85 years old or older, being dependent in five or more activities of daily living, and taking two or more psychotropic drugs
paragraphs.note: The three admission variables that make up the rule, exactly as the claim describes.

paragraphs.context: The scores for the clinical prediction rule were assigned on the basis of regression coefficients obtained in the logistic regression model ( table 7 ). One point was given to patients older than 85 years, to those who had two or more points in the variable drugs, and to those with impairments in five or more of the ADL considered. Therefore, the total score for the rule ranged between 0 and 3.
paragraphs.highlight: Therefore, the total score for the rule ranged between 0 and 3
paragraphs.note: One point per criterion gives a total ranging 0-3, matching the claim's 0-3 points.

paragraphs.context: The clinical prediction rule was applied to the validation cohort. We report the incidence of delirium as a function of score on the rule and the ORs using the lowest risk category as the reference. The performance of the rule in the two cohorts was explored using receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

paragraphs.note: Delirium incidence is reported by score band (4%/14%/43% by score 0/1/2 in the derivation cohort), i.e. the score is banded to predicted incidence.

paragraphs.context: This rule may facilitate early identification of high risk patients and target early initiation of preventive measures.
paragraphs.highlight: target early initiation of preventive measures
paragraphs.note: The rule's stated purpose is to flag high-risk patients so preventive measures can begin early — i.e. to target the prevention bundle.

paragraphs.context: The association between delirium and an increase of morbidity and mortality 5 6 9 is well known, as are the effectiveness of preventive measures to avoid the development of the disease. 15–18 The use of the proposed predictive rule would allow us to classify around half of our inpatients (53%) as high risk. Taking preventative measures in this high-risk group, up to 93.4% of those who developed delirium in our study would have been covered by the measures and might not have then developed the condition.
paragraphs.highlight: Taking preventative measures in this high-risk group, up to 93.4% of those who developed delirium in our study would have been covered by the measures
paragraphs.note: Applying the rule classifies ~53% as high-risk and would have covered 93.4% of eventual delirium cases with preventive measures, supporting its use to target prevention.

paragraphs.context: Older people and people with dementia, severe illness or a hip fracture are more at risk of delirium. The prevalence of delirium in people on medical wards in hospital is about 20% to 30%, and 10% to 50% of people having surgery develop delirium. In long-term care the prevalence is under 20%. But reporting of delirium is poor in the UK, indicating that awareness and reporting procedures need to be improved.

claims.synthesis: Martinez 2012 directly supports every element of the claim — three admission-measurable variables (age >=85, dependence in >=5 ADL, >=2 psychotropic-drug points) summed to a 0-3 score whose bands map to rising delirium incidence, derived and validated on internal-medicine ward admissions to target early prevention. NICE CG103 agrees with the underlying principle of assessing admission risk to trigger a multicomponent prevention bundle, but its own risk model (any one of age >=65, cognitive impairment, hip fracture, or severe illness) is a broader, non-scored scheme, so Martinez remains the governing on-scope source for the specific validated 0-3 prediction rule the claim describes.

paragraphs.context: Results Delirium developed in 9.9 percent of the intervention group, as compared with 15.0 percent of the usual-care group (matched odds ratio, 0.60; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.39 to 0.92). The total number of days with delirium (105 vs. 161, P=0.02) and the total number of episodes (62 vs. 90, P=0.03) were significantly lower in the intervention group. However, the severity of delirium and recurrence rates were not significantly different. The overall rate of adherence to the intervention was 87 percent, and the total number of targeted risk factors per patient was significantly reduced. Intervention was associated with significant improvement in the degree of cognitive impairment among patients with cognitive impairment at admission and with a significant reduction in the rate of use of sleep medications among all patients. Among the other risk factors, there were trends toward improvement in immobility, visual impairment, and hearing impairment. Conclusions The risk-factor intervention strategy that we studied resulted in significant reductions in the number and duration of episodes of delirium in hospitalized older patients. The intervention had no significant effect on the severity of delirium or on recurrence rates; this finding suggests that primary prevention of delirium is probably the most effective treatment strategy. (N Engl J Med 1999;340:669-76.)

paragraphs.context: Methods We studied 852 patients 70 years of age or older who had been admitted to the general-medicine service at a teaching hospital. Patients from one intervention unit and two usual-care units were enrolled by means of a prospective matching strategy. The intervention consisted of standardized protocols for the management of six risk factors for delirium: cognitive impairment, sleep deprivation, immobility, visual impairment, hearing impairment, and dehydration. Delirium, the primary outcome, was assessed daily until discharge.

paragraphs.context: MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES We identified 14 interventional studies. The results for outcomes of delirium incidence, falls, length of stay, and institutionalization were pooled for the meta-analysis, but heterogeneity limited our meta-analysis of the results for change in functional or cognitive status. Overall, 11 studies demonstrated significant reductions in delirium incidence (odds ratio [OR], 0.47; 95% CI, 0.38-0.58). Four randomized or matched trials reduced delirium incidence by 44% (OR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.42-0.76). The rate of falls decreased significantly among intervention patients in 4 studies (OR, 0.38; 95% CI, 0.25-0.60); in 2 randomized or matched trials, the rate of falls was reduced by 64% (OR, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.22-0.61). Length of stay and institutionalization also trended toward decreases in the intervention groups, with a mean difference of -0.16 (95% CI, -0.97 to 0.64) day shorter and the odds of institutionalization 5% lower (OR, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.71-1.26). Among higher-quality randomized or matched trials, length of stay trended -0.33 (95% CI, -1.38 to 0.72) day shorter, and the odds of institutionalization trended 6% lower (OR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.69-1.30).

paragraphs.note: Pooled effect of multicomponent nonpharmacological interventions on delirium incidence (OR 0.47).

The NNT in the combined sample was 14.3 (95% CI, 11.1-20.0).

The NNTs were 20.0 (95% CI, 12.5-33.3) among RMTs and 11.1 (95% CI, 8.316.7) among non-RMTs. Delirium incidence was also stratified by patient type (eFigure 2 in the Supplement).

paragraphs.context: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE Multicomponent nonpharmacological delirium prevention interventions are effective in reducing delirium incidence and preventing falls, with a trend toward decreasing length of stay and avoiding institutionalization. Given the current focus on prevention of hospital-based complications and improved cost-effectiveness of care, this meta-analysis supports the use of these interventions to advance acute care for older persons.

paragraphs.context: Data Synthesis: A total of 14 RCTs were included. There were no differences in delirium incidence or duration, hospital length of stay (high strength of evidence [SOE]), and mortality between haloperidol and placebo used for delirium prevention. Little to no evidence was found to determine the effect of haloperidol on cognitive function, delirium severity (insufficient SOE), inappropriate continuation, and sedation (insufficient SOE).

We found no difference in the RR for delirium with haloperidol compared with placebo (0.94 [CI, 0.77 to 1.16]) (Figure 3; Supplement Figure 3 and Supplement Table 9, available at Annals.org).

Antipsychotics were not associated with improvements short-term mortality, severity or duration of delirium, and length of ICU and hospital stay. However, existing studies demonstrate heterogeneity in study design, including diverse populations, with few studies focused specifically on older postoperative patients. paragraphs.context: Results--Screening of 10,877 eligible records identified 19 studies. In seven studies comparing antipsychotics to placebo or no treatment for delirium prevention in postoperative patients, there was no significant effect on delirium incidence (OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.23, 1.34; I2 = 93%). Using data reported from all 19 studies, antipsychotic use was not associated with change in delirium duration, severity, hospital or ICU LOS, with high heterogeneity among studies. claims.synthesis: The primary on-scope source, Siddiqi 2016 (Cochrane, hospitalised non-ICU patients), directly supports both prongs — multicomponent interventions cut incident delirium (RR 0.69) while antipsychotics as a class show no clear benefit — and it governs because it is the exact population and figure the claim cites; it is corroborated for the bundle by Inouye 1999 and Hshieh 2015 and for antipsychotics by Oh 2019 and Neufeld 2016. The only divergence is scope, not direction: atypical/second-generation antipsychotics reduced incidence in postoperative surgical trials (Siddiqi's olanzapine subgroup and Oh's second-generation pooled RR 0.36), and the AGS 2015 postoperative guideline rates prophylactic antipsychotics as "insufficient evidence" rather than clearly ineffective — a different surgical setting/agent that should not be read as endorsing routine antipsychotic prophylaxis in general non-ICU inpatients.

claims.statement: Ten-component HELP-style bundle: reorientation; glasses & hearing aids; early mobilisation; sleep protocol; hydration & nutrition; deliriogenic/anticholinergic medication review; pain treated without over-sedation; bowel/bladder care; infection/hypoxia/metabolic work-up; family engagement & education.
claims.passage:
Nonpharmacologic interventions to prevent postoperative delirium may include the following elements: cognitive reorientation, sleep enhancement (i.e., nonpharmacologic sleep protocol and sleep hygiene), early mobility and/or physical rehabilitation, adaptations for visual and hearing impairment, nutrition and fluid repletion, pain management, appropriate medication usage, adequate oxygenation, and prevention of constipation.
Also Siddiqi 2016 (Cochrane) (p. 16): “Risk factors that have so far been identified include: increased age, sensory deprivation (visual or hearing impairment), sleep deprivation, social isolation, physical restraint, use of bladder catheter, iatrogenic adverse events, poly-pharmacy (more than three new medications added), use of psychoactive drugs, co-morbidities, severe illness (especially infection, fracture or stroke), prior cognitive impairment, temperature abnormality (fever or hypothermia), dehydration, malnutrition and low serum albumin”
Composite (HELP-style). AGS 2015 (p. 4) lists most components verbatim — cognitive reorientation, sleep enhancement, early mobility, adaptations for visual/hearing impairment, nutrition and fluid repletion, pain management, appropriate medication use, adequate oxygenation, prevention of constipation. Siddiqi 2016 frames the same as modifiable risk factors (adds physical restraint and bladder catheter; p. 16). A few card specifics — whiteboard/clock/calendar, eye mask/earplugs, family engagement & delirium education — trace to the Hospital Elder Life Program (Inouye 1999) and Hshieh 2015, which the tool cites but which are not held in the local reference archive.

paragraphs.context: On the basis of seven randomised controlled trials (RCTs) (four in medical patients and three in surgical patients) n = 1950 participants, there is moderate-quality evidence that multicomponent delirium prevention interventions can reduce rates of incident delirium; this is consistent across the included trials. Evidence has been downgraded due to the possibility of performance bias (the nature of the intervention precludes blinding of participants and those delivering intervention). Outcome assessors were unblinded to the intervention in two studies, including the study with the largest weighting and highest event rate. Furthermore, there is a risk of other bias in two of the included studies due to an imbalance between the intervention and control groups in respect to the prevalence of pre-existing dementia.

paragraphs.context: Preliminary evidence for the content of multicomponent interventions suggests that they should include as a minimum: sta education; individualised care (sometimes referred to as person-centred care); re-orientation at frequent intervals; and early mobilisation, but this needs further investigation. These areas are familiar aspects of care but are currently poorly and unreliably delivered.

paragraphs.context: There are many risk factors for developing delirium (e.g. infection, dehydration, certain medications). Therefore, one approach (called `multi-component interventions') to preventing delirium is to target these multiple risk factors. Some medications have e ects on the brain chemicals implicated in developing delirium, and may, therefore, have a role in prevention. There are also a number of other interventions that target delirium risk factors related to anaesthesia and medical treatment around the time of surgery.
paragraphs.highlight: There are many risk factors for developing delirium (e.g. infection, dehydration, certain medications).
paragraphs.note: Rationale for the bundle — targeting multiple modifiable risk factors (infection, dehydration, medications) underpins the work-up, hydration, and medication-review components.

paragraphs.context: Research in older people has identified a range of risk factors for delirium. The condition clearly has a multi-factorial aetiology, and these risk factors interact (Inouye 1998b); the more risk factors that are present, the greater the likelihood that the patient will develop delirium. Risk factors that have so far been identified include: increased age, sensory deprivation (visual or hearing impairment), sleep deprivation, social isolation, physical restraint, use of bladder catheter, iatrogenic adverse events, poly-pharmacy (more than three new medications added), use of psychoactive drugs, comorbidities, severe illness (especially infection, fracture or stroke), prior cognitive impairment, temperature abnormality (fever or hypothermia), dehydration, malnutrition and low serum albumin (Inouye 1998b; Inouye 1999c; NICE 2010).
paragraphs.highlight: use of bladder catheter, iatrogenic adverse events, poly-pharmacy (more than three new medications added)
paragraphs.note: The risk-factor list grounds several otherwise weakly-cited components — bladder catheters, polypharmacy, sensory deprivation, sleep, and infection are all recognised delirium risk factors.

Evidence for Recommendation: Relevant medications or medication classes include benzodiazepines, anticholinergics (e.g., cyclobenzaprine, oxybutynin, prochlorperazine, promethazine, tricyclic antidepressants, paroxetine and drugs with high anticholinergic properties), diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, histamine2-receptor antagonists (e.g., cimetidine), sedative-hypnotics, and meperidine. claims.synthesis: All four sources support a HELP-style multicomponent nonpharmacological prevention bundle for hospitalised older adults and none contradicts the claim: the AGS 2015 postoperative-delirium guideline (primary anchor, p. 4) governs the specific list, enumerating nearly all ten components in one strong recommendation, while Inouye 1999 (HELP) and Hshieh 2015 establish and meta-analytically validate the core six (reorientation, sleep, mobilisation, vision/hearing, hydration) and Siddiqi 2016 confirms multicomponent prevention works in the exact hospitalised non-ICU (step-down) setting. The four extra components (medication review, pain without over-sedation, bowel/bladder care, infection/hypoxia/metabolic work-up, family engagement) rest chiefly on the AGS enumeration — drawn from an older-surgical population — rather than on all four sources, so the AGS list is the governing citation for the full ten while the HELP trials cover only the core six.

claims.statement: Review deliriogenic / anticholinergic medications first — minimise the burden.
claims.passage:
A high anticholinergic burden within 24 hours after admission was significantly associated with incident delirium. Although prospective studies need to confirm these results, discontinuing or substituting drugs with a score of ≥3 at admission might be a targeted intervention to reduce incident delirium.
Also AGS 2015 (postoperative delirium guideline) (p. 8): “The prescribing practitioner should avoid medications that induce delirium postoperatively in older adults to prevent delirium (strength of recommendation: strong; quality of evidence: low).”
Also AGS 2015 (postoperative delirium guideline) (p. 8): “Current evidence most strongly associates use of anticholinergic drugs, meperidine and benzodiazepines with increased postoperative delirium.”
Supported. Lisibach 2022 found high anticholinergic burden within 24 h of admission was significantly associated with incident delirium and that discontinuing/substituting high-burden drugs is a plausible reducing intervention (p. 1). AGS 2015 issues a strong recommendation to avoid deliriogenic medications and names anticholinergics among the drugs most strongly associated with postoperative delirium (p. 8). 'First' is the card's operational ordering.

paragraphs.context: A cumulative ACH burden score of three points or more can be considered a high burden, which was statistically significantly and independently associated with the development of delirium during hospitalisation. The ABSs are convenient clinical tools to measure the ACH burden in hospitalised patients. Newer high‐quality ABSs built from previously published scales seem to perform better. However, cut‐off values might differ depending on the scale and outcome studied. Discontinuing or substituting drugs with an ACH score of three points or more upon admission might be a targeted intervention to reduce the risk of delirium development. However, it should be noted that delirium is a multifactorial syndrome, and that drugs are only one factor to be considered in delirium prevention. Further studies should be conducted in order to prospectively verify whether discontinuing drugs with ACH properties might reduce delirium occurrences.

claims.synthesis: Both sources endorse reviewing and minimising deliriogenic/anticholinergic medications to reduce delirium. Lisibach 2022 is the on-scope, governing source for a general step-down/ward card: in older hospitalised (non-ICU) patients a high cumulative anticholinergic burden was independently associated with incident delirium, and discontinuing or substituting high-burden drugs is presented as a targeted preventive intervention (with the caveat that drugs are only one factor in a multifactorial syndrome). AGS 2015 corroborates the same principle — a strong recommendation to avoid anticholinergic/deliriogenic drugs and to evaluate medications to identify causes — but from a different population (postoperative older surgical patients), so it is a nearest-match at a different scope rather than direct on-scope support.

claims.synthesis: Both guidelines directly support the card's core action — AGS 2015 Recommendation IV (p.5, the primary anchor) and NICE CG103 1.7.1 (p.11, a [2010] recommendation that remains the current position after the 2023 focused update on assessment) each direct clinicians to perform a medical evaluation and identify/manage the underlying cause(s) once delirium is diagnosed — but both state this generically. paragraphs.context: There is strong evidence supporting multi-component interventions to prevent delirium in hospitalised patients. There is no clear evidence that cholinesterase inhibitors, antipsychotic medication or melatonin reduce the incidence of delirium. Using the Bispectral Index to monitor and control depth of anaesthesia reduces the incidence of postoperative delirium. The role of drugs and other anaesthetic techniques to prevent delirium remains uncertain.

paragraphs.note: Abstract authors' conclusions: strong evidence for the multicomponent bundle, contrasted with no clear benefit from cholinesterase inhibitors, antipsychotics, or melatonin.

paragraphs.context: Seven studies (2018 participants) evaluated non-pharmacological multi-component interventions (Abizanda 2011; Bonaventura 2007; Hempenius 2013; Je s 2013; Lundstrom 2007; Marcantonio 2001; Martinez 2012) in comparison to usual care. Individual components of each multi-component intervention are summarised in Table 1. The number of components varied between two (Je s 2013) and 13 (Hempenius 2013) (Table 1). Most included individualised care, an educational component, reorientation, and early mobilisation. Many of the delirium risk factors targeted with multi-component interventions relate to good basic care. The nature in which interventions were implemented varied between the studies: some relied on a protocol-driven approach (Bonaventura 2007; Je s 2013; Marcantonio 2001), whilst others were more pragmatic in the delivery of the intervention (e.g. the family delivered the reorientation intervention in Martinez 2012). Two studies were based on therapist interventions (Abizanda 2011; Je s 2013), one was multidisciplinary including a Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (Lundstrom 2007), and two were based on proactive perioperative input from a geriatrician (Hempenius 2013; Marcantonio 2001).
paragraphs.highlight: Most included individualised care, an educational component, reorientation, and early mobilisation
paragraphs.note: Describes what the bundle contains — the components common to the seven trials — grounding what 'the multicomponent bundle' means.

paragraphs.context: Multi-component interventions for delirium prevention are now also recognised and recommended in practice guidelines. The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines for delirium were published in 2010 (NICE 2010). These identified multi-component interventions as having a critical role in identifying and addressing modifiable, clinical risk factors for delirium prevention. Multi-component assessment and intervention is recommended within 24 hours of admission for those at risk; the intervention should be personalised to the needs of the individual and delivered by a multidisciplinary team (NICE 2010). Cost savings are identified to be anticipated, although we found no data on this in our review.
paragraphs.highlight: Multi-component assessment and intervention is recommended within 24 hours of admission for those at risk
paragraphs.note: Nearest match on timing/eligibility (NICE): the intervention is recommended for those 'at risk,' a narrower target than the claim's 'every patient.'

paragraphs.context: Results Delirium developed in 9.9 percent of the intervention group, as compared with 15.0 percent of the usual-care group (matched odds ratio, 0.60; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.39 to 0.92). The total number of days with delirium (105 vs. 161, P=0.02) and the total number of episodes (62 vs. 90, P=0.03) were significantly lower in the intervention group. However, the severity of delirium and recurrence rates were not significantly different. The overall rate of adherence to the intervention was 87 percent, and the total number of targeted risk factors per patient was significantly reduced. Intervention was associated with significant improvement in the degree of cognitive impairment among patients with cognitive impairment at admission and with a significant reduction in the rate of use of sleep medications among all patients. Among the other risk factors, there were trends toward improvement in immobility, visual impairment, and hearing impairment. Conclusions The risk-factor intervention strategy that we studied resulted in significant reductions in the number and duration of episodes of delirium in hospitalized older patients. The intervention had no significant effect on the severity of delirium or on recurrence rates; this finding suggests that primary prevention of delirium is probably the most effective treatment strategy. (N Engl J Med 1999;340:669-76.)
paragraphs.highlight: primary prevention of delirium is probably the most effective treatment strategy
paragraphs.note: Because severity and recurrence of established delirium were unchanged, the authors conclude the bundle's value is as first-line primary prevention.

paragraphs.context: Methods We studied 852 patients 70 years of age or older who had been admitted to the general-medicine service at a teaching hospital. Patients from one intervention unit and two usual-care units were enrolled by means of a prospective matching strategy. The intervention consisted of standardized protocols for the management of six risk factors for delirium: cognitive impairment, sleep deprivation, immobility, visual impairment, hearing impairment, and dehydration. Delirium, the primary outcome, was assessed daily until discharge.
paragraphs.highlight: 852 patients 70 years of age or older who had been admitted to the general-medicine service
paragraphs.note: Population is older (≥70) general-medicine inpatients enrolled by intermediate/high delirium risk — not literally 'every patient,' and not a step-down cohort.

paragraphs.context: Recommendation--Healthcare systems and hospitals should implement multicomponent nonpharmacologic intervention programs delivered by an interdisciplinary team (including physicians, nurses, and possibly other healthcare professionals) for the entire hospitalization in at-risk older adults undergoing surgery to prevent delirium (strength of recommendation: strong; quality of evidence: moderate).

paragraphs.note: Recommendation II — a strong recommendation to implement the multicomponent non-pharmacologic bundle to prevent delirium; setting is postoperative at-risk surgical older adults.

paragraphs.context: B. Potential Harms of All Nonpharmacologic Recommendations: No harmful effects of nonpharmacologic approaches to delirium prevention or management have been reported, other than costs of program resources, which may be offset by the considerable costs of delirium. Cost-effectiveness of multicomponent delirium intervention strategies in a variety of settings has been demonstrated.
paragraphs.highlight: No harmful effects of nonpharmacologic approaches to delirium prevention or management have been reported
paragraphs.note: Directly supports 'manage without new harm': the non-pharmacologic approaches carry no reported harms.

paragraphs.context: The criteria used by the panel to designate the strength of recommendation appear in Table S1. In all cases, the strength of recommendation was based on carefully balancing the benefits of treatment against the potential harms. For example, strong recommendations were made when the panel determined that the benefits clearly outweighed harms (such as with nonpharmacologic interventions) or when the potential harms clearly outweighed the benefits (such as with benzodiazepine treatment).
paragraphs.highlight: the benefits clearly outweighed harms (such as with nonpharmacologic interventions)
paragraphs.note: Grades non-pharmacologic interventions as benefits-outweigh-harms (strong) versus benzodiazepines as harms-outweigh-benefits — supports non-pharm as the safe first-line.

paragraphs.context: Recommendation--Healthcare professionals should consider multicomponent interventions implemented by an interdisciplinary team in older adults diagnosed with postoperative delirium to improve clinical outcomes (strength of recommendation: weak; quality of evidence: low).
paragraphs.highlight: to improve clinical outcomes (strength of recommendation: weak; quality of evidence: low)
paragraphs.note: Recommendation III — nearest match to the 'Manage' scope, but for treating established delirium the multicomponent bundle is only a weak, low-quality recommendation (vs strong for prevention).

paragraphs.context: Recommendation--The prescribing practitioner should not use benzodiazepines as a first-line treatment of the agitated postoperative delirious patient who is threatening substantial harm to self and/or others to treat postoperative delirium except when benzodiazepines are specifically indicated (including, but not limited to, treatment of alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal). Treatment with benzodiazepines should be at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible duration, and should be employed only if behavioral measures have failed or are not possible and ongoing use should be evaluated daily with inperson examination of the patient (strength of recommendation: strong; quality of evidence: low).
paragraphs.highlight: should not use benzodiazepines as a first-line treatment
paragraphs.note: Different intervention (benzodiazepines), included because it explicitly reserves pharmacologic agents as non-first-line, reinforcing that the non-pharm bundle comes first.

claims.synthesis: All three sources agree that a multicomponent non-pharmacologic bundle is the recommended, harm-free first-line intervention for delirium; Siddiqi 2016 — the only source covering hospitalised non-ICU medical and surgical wards, the closest match to a step-down setting — governs and concludes these interventions should be adopted into routine care. The supporting evidence is strongest for primary prevention in at-risk patients (Inouye's HELP RCT was in older ≥70 general-medicine inpatients; AGS gives a strong prevention recommendation but only a weak one for treating established postoperative delirium), so "first-line for every patient" is a reasonable extrapolation of the consensus rather than a directly tested claim.

claims.section: Act card — Manage without new harm
claims.statement: Antipsychotics do NOT prevent or treat delirium — do not use them routinely.
claims.passage:
Conclusion—Antipsychotics for prevention or treatment of delirium is not supported by current evidence.
Also Nikooie 2019 (antipsychotics — treatment) (p. 1): “Conclusion: Current evidence does not support routine use of haloperidol or second-generation antipsychotics to treat delirium in adult inpatients.”
Also Nikooie 2019 (antipsychotics — treatment) (p. 9): “In conclusion, antipsychotics for treatment of delirium in adult inpatients did not improve patient outcomes, with little evidence of neurologic harms but a tendency for more frequent potentially harmful cardiac effects.”
Supported on both limbs. Neufeld 2016 concludes antipsychotics for prevention or treatment of delirium are not supported by current evidence (p. 2). Nikooie 2019 concludes current evidence does not support routine antipsychotics to treat delirium and that treatment did not improve outcomes (p. 1, p. 9); Oh 2019 (prevention) is cited on the prevention card.

perSource.label: Neufeld 2016 (antipsychotics meta-analysis)
perSource.cite: Neufeld KJ, et al. Antipsychotic medication for prevention and treatment of delirium in hospitalized adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Am Geriatr Soc 2016;64:705.
perSource.note: Primary source; the only one covering BOTH halves of the claim (prevention and treatment) in hospitalized adults, and it concludes the practice is unsupported.

paragraphs.context: Conclusion--Antipsychotics for prevention or treatment of delirium is not supported by current evidence. Additional methodologically rigorous studies using standardized outcome measures are needed.
paragraphs.highlight: Antipsychotics for prevention or treatment of delirium is not supported by current evidence.
paragraphs.note: Abstract conclusion (the cited primaryAnchor, p. 2) directly supporting the card statement for both prevention and treatment.

paragraphs.context: There is insufficient evidence currently to support the routine use of antipsychotic pharmacotherapy to prevent or treat delirium in hospitalized adult patients, including in the postoperative setting. There is a great need to standardize outcome measures via creation of a core outcome set for delirium prevention and treatment trials and conduct of additional rigorous well-powered RCTs in high risk populations.
paragraphs.highlight: There is insufficient evidence currently to support the routine use of antipsychotic pharmacotherapy to prevent or treat delirium in hospitalized adult patients, including in the postoperative setting.
paragraphs.note: Concluding paragraph uses the exact 'routine use' framing that matches the card's 'do not use them routinely.'

paragraphs.context: This systematic review and meta-analysis suggests that antipsychotic pharmacotherapy does not improve outcomes when used for prevention or treatment of delirium in hospitalized adult patients. Antipsychotics were not associated with improvements short-term mortality, severity or duration of delirium, and length of ICU and hospital stay. However, existing studies demonstrate heterogeneity in study design, including diverse populations, with few studies focused specifically on older postoperative patients. There was substantial variability in outcome measures with few postoperative studies evaluating mortality and functional outcomes.
paragraphs.highlight: antipsychotic pharmacotherapy does not improve outcomes when used for prevention or treatment of delirium in hospitalized adult patients
paragraphs.note: Discussion synthesis reiterating no benefit for either indication.

paragraphs.context: Results--Screening of 10,877 eligible records identified 19 studies. In seven studies comparing antipsychotics to placebo or no treatment for delirium prevention in postoperative patients, there was no significant effect on delirium incidence (OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.23, 1.34; I2 = 93%). Using data reported from all 19 studies, antipsychotic use was not associated with change in delirium duration, severity, hospital or ICU LOS, with high heterogeneity among studies. No association with mortality was detected (OR 0.90; 95% CI 0.62, 1.29; I2 = 0%).
paragraphs.highlight: there was no significant effect on delirium incidence
paragraphs.note: Abstract Results giving the meta-analytic basis (no effect on incidence, duration, severity, LOS, mortality).

paragraphs.context: Careful reflection on which outcomes are most meaningful to clinicians and patients should also inform future research. While antipsychotics in this review do not appear to decrease the incidence of delirium in the postoperative period, or improve other outcomes when used to treat delirious adult inpatients, none of the studies evaluated symptomatic relief attributable to these medications. Decreasing patient agitation and distress is a common reason for the prescription of antipsychotics in hospitalized adults and yet the field has no uniform data on those outcomes. Much more work in this area is needed to delineate the best strategies around delirium prevention, particularly in high-risk populations such as older postoperative patients. Well-powered randomized controlled evaluations, particularly among older at-risk patients immediately post-anesthesia, with well-defined outcomes are warranted in order to better understand whether there is any benefit from these medications.
paragraphs.highlight: none of the studies evaluated symptomatic relief attributable to these medications
paragraphs.note: Nearest-match caveat: the reviewed evidence did not assess short-term symptomatic (agitation/distress) relief, so 'do not use routinely' addresses preventing/treating the delirium syndrome, not acute agitation control — must not be over-read as covering that indication.

perSource.label: Oh 2019 (antipsychotics — prevention)
perSource.cite: Oh ES, et al. Antipsychotics for preventing delirium in hospitalized adults: a systematic review. Ann Intern Med 2019;171:474.
perSource.note: Covers only the PREVENTION half of the claim, and carries a genuine subgroup exception (second-generation antipsychotics in postoperative surgery), so it partially qualifies the blanket 'do not prevent.'

paragraphs.context: Conclusion: Current evidence does not support routine use of haloperidol or second-generation antipsychotics for prevention of delirium. There is limited evidence that second-generation antipsychotics may lower the incidence of delirium in postoperative patients, but more research is needed. Future trials should use standardized outcome measures.
paragraphs.highlight: Current evidence does not support routine use of haloperidol or second-generation antipsychotics for prevention of delirium.
paragraphs.note: Abstract conclusion; governs the prevention half of the card statement.

paragraphs.context: Our systematic review of 14 RCTs (4281 participants) found insufficient or no evidence supporting the routine use of antipsychotics for the prevention of delirium in adult inpatients.
paragraphs.highlight: found insufficient or no evidence supporting the routine use of antipsychotics for the prevention of delirium in adult inpatients
paragraphs.note: Opening of Discussion restating the primary finding across 14 RCTs.

paragraphs.context: In conclusion, evidence was insufficient to support the routine use of antipsychotics for preventing delirium in adult patients. Second-generation antipsychotics may lower delirium incidence in postoperative patients, but more research is needed to confirm this finding. Although statistically significant differences were not detected in cardiac side effects when antipsychotics were compared with placebo, in some of the trials, events were more common in patients receiving an antipsychotic.
paragraphs.highlight: evidence was insufficient to support the routine use of antipsychotics for preventing delirium in adult patients
paragraphs.note: Closing conclusion, verbatim support for 'do not use routinely' in prevention.

paragraphs.context: Three RCTs with varying ROB (30, 31, 39) (627 participants) compared delirium incidence with secondgeneration antipsychotics (olanzapine, risperidone) versus placebo in on-pump cardiac or joint-replacement surgery. We found a statistically significant and clinically meaningful difference favoring second-generation antipsychotics in the pooled analysis (RR, 0.36 [CI, 0.26 to 0.50]) (Figure 3; Supplement Figure 3 and Supplement Table 9).
paragraphs.highlight: We found a statistically significant and clinically meaningful difference favoring second-generation antipsychotics in the pooled analysis (RR, 0.36 [CI, 0.26 to 0.50])
paragraphs.note: Nearest match that must NOT be read as blanket support: in postoperative on-pump cardiac / joint-replacement surgery patients, second-generation antipsychotics (not haloperidol) lowered delirium incidence — limited evidence the authors flag as needing confirmation; a subgroup exception, not a treatment finding.

perSource.label: Nikooie 2019 (antipsychotics — treatment)
perSource.cite: Nikooie R, et al. Antipsychotics for treating delirium in hospitalized adults: a systematic review. Ann Intern Med 2019;171:485.
perSource.note: Covers only the TREATMENT half of the claim; every treatment comparison showed no benefit or harm, so it fully supports 'do not routinely treat delirium with antipsychotics.'

paragraphs.context: Conclusion: Current evidence does not support routine use of haloperidol or second-generation antipsychotics to treat delirium in adult inpatients.
paragraphs.highlight: Current evidence does not support routine use of haloperidol or second-generation antipsychotics to treat delirium in adult inpatients.
paragraphs.note: Abstract conclusion; governs the treatment half of the card statement.

paragraphs.context: Our systematic review of 26 RCTs and observational studies, evaluating 5607 adult inpatients with delirium, does not support routine use of haloperidol or second-generation antipsychotics for treating delirium in adult inpatients.
paragraphs.highlight: does not support routine use of haloperidol or second-generation antipsychotics for treating delirium in adult inpatients
paragraphs.note: Opening sentence of the Discussion, summarizing 26 studies / 5607 inpatients.

paragraphs.context: In conclusion, antipsychotics for treatment of delirium in adult inpatients did not improve patient outcomes, with little evidence of neurologic harms but a tendency for more frequent potentially harmful cardiac effects. For some clinically important outcomes and specific patient subgroups (such as older adults and palliative care patients), there was insufficient or no evidence, emphasizing the need for continued future research in the field.
paragraphs.highlight: antipsychotics for treatment of delirium in adult inpatients did not improve patient outcomes
paragraphs.note: Closing conclusion; adds that harmful cardiac effects tended to occur more frequently.

paragraphs.context: Moreover, a single RCT in 249 palliative care patients (37) reported that haloperidol and risperidone had less improvement in delirium severity and more extrapyramidal symptoms compared with placebo, with haloperidol (versus placebo) demonstrating significantly worse survival.
paragraphs.highlight: haloperidol (versus placebo) demonstrating significantly worse survival
paragraphs.note: Nearest-match different population: in palliative-care patients the single RCT showed antipsychotics were WORSE than placebo (less severity improvement, more EPS, worse survival) — an active-harm signal specific to that population, reinforcing 'do not use routinely' rather than contradicting it.

claims.synthesis: All three systematic reviews agree that current evidence does not support the routine use of antipsychotics to prevent (Oh 2019) or treat (Nikooie 2019) delirium in hospitalized adults, and the primary source, Neufeld 2016 — which addresses both indications — reaches the same conclusion, so the card statement is well grounded and governed by Neufeld 2016. The only qualifications are nearest-match subgroups that must not be read as endorsement: Oh 2019's limited-evidence finding that second-generation antipsychotics (not haloperidol) may lower delirium incidence specifically in postoperative surgical patients, Nikooie 2019's palliative-care signal of net harm, and Neufeld 2016's caveat that none of the trials evaluated short-term symptomatic relief of agitation/distress.

paragraphs.context: The RASS is an arousal scale commonly used in intensive care units to assess for depth of sedation (Figure 1),10 but has been incorporated into several delirium assessments to assess for level of consciousness.6 For this study, we replaced the term "sedation" with "drowsy," (Figure 1) to describe level of consciousness regardless of sedation administration. A RASS of 0 represented normal level of consciousness whereas a RASS other than 0 represented the presence of altered level of consciousness. The RASS was determined by an emergency physician (EP) and research assistants (RAs; college graduates, emergency medical technicians, and paramedics). Before the study began, the RAs were given a 5-minute didactic lecture about the RASS. The principal investigator then observed them perform the RASS in five older ED patients and provided them instruction if there was any discordance.

paragraphs.context: Postoperative day one through three index testing was obtained by two independent examiners who engaged the patients on that day. These examiners were both residents and nursing staff. For reference rating, patients were assessed for POD by an experienced reference-rater once every day. The reference-raters used DSM-5 criteria, Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS), CAM-ICU and features of disorientation for diagnosing POD. The reference rater was allowed to make his diagnosis based on all the diagnostic criteria and his professional experience. The reference raters were experienced senior consultants in intensive care (BER, UG) and geriatrics (TZ). Clinical information, e.g. nurses’ notes and electronic medical records, was available to all examiners. All examination results were blinded in a sealed box. No examiner had knowledge about other index test results or preoperative cognitive testing. The examinations were carried out alongside the morning ward round without no more than 60 min in between examinations.

paragraphs.note: Shows RASS is part of the delirium workup in this step-down cohort, but this methods sentence does not describe the -4/-5 assessability gate.

paragraphs.context: By creating the CAM-IMC flowchart design as a point-based scoring system, the importance of disorientation as a central feature of POD has been reinforced. The features disorientation and inattention can each trigger a positive test result. The system assigns up to five points for disorientation and three points for inattention, thereby increasing the weight of these single features in the overall diagnosis. The categories of acute or fluctuating change and RASS≠0 have been reduced in significance and each contribute one point to the total score but are not mandatory for a positive test outcome. This is reflected in their limited ability to discriminate POD, as shown by a distinct lower AUROC compared to disorientation, inattention and overall CAM-IMC. As a result, disorientation and inattention exert the greatest influence on CAM-IMC test-results. In comparison, the CAM-ICU does not diagnose POD if “Acute change or fluctuating course of the mental status” is assessed as negative, even when inattention or disorganized thinking” is present. By employing a point-based scoring system, the CAM-IMC avoids this limitation.

paragraphs.note: Here RASS is used as a low-weight delirium scoring feature (RASS not equal to 0), a different role than the arousal gate that decides whether a patient is assessable at all.

paragraphs.context: The RASS is an arousal scale commonly used in intensive care units to assess for depth of sedation (Figure 1),10 but has been incorporated into several delirium assessments to assess for level of consciousness.6 For this study, we replaced the term "sedation" with "drowsy," (Figure 1) to describe level of consciousness regardless of sedation administration. A RASS of 0 represented normal level of consciousness whereas a RASS other than 0 represented the presence of altered level of consciousness. The RASS was determined by an emergency physician (EP) and research assistants (RAs; college graduates, emergency medical technicians, and paramedics). Before the study began, the RAs were given a 5-minute didactic lecture about the RASS. The principal investigator then observed them perform the RASS in five older ED patients and provided them instruction if there was any discordance.

The first patient who met all the eligibility criteria was enrolled each day. The 12 hour cut-off was used to include patients who presented to the ED in the evening and early morning hours. Patients were excluded if they were non-English speaking, deaf or blind, previously enrolled, non-verbal or unable to follow simple commands prior to their acute illnesses, comatose, or did not complete all the study assessments. paragraphs.context: We found multi-component interventions reduced the incidence of delirium compared to usual care (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.81; seven studies; 1950 participants; moderate-quality evidence). E ect sizes were similar in medical (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.92; four studies; 1365 participants) and surgical settings (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.85; three studies; 585 participants). In the subgroup of patients with preexisting dementia, the e ect of multi-component interventions remains uncertain (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.36; one study, 50 participants; low-quality evidence).

paragraphs.context: There is strong evidence supporting multi-component interventions to prevent delirium in hospitalised patients.
