paragraphs.context: Results Delirium developed in 9.9 percent of the intervention group, as compared with 15.0 percent of the usual-care group (matched odds ratio, 0.60; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.39 to 0.92). The total number of days with delirium (105 vs. 161, P=0.02) and the total number of episodes (62 vs. 90, P=0.03) were significantly lower in the intervention group. However, the severity of delirium and recurrence rates were not significantly different. The overall rate of adherence to the intervention was 87 percent, and the total number of targeted risk factors per patient was significantly reduced. Intervention was associated with significant improvement in the degree of cognitive impairment among patients with cognitive impairment at admission and with a significant reduction in the rate of use of sleep medications among all patients. Among the other risk factors, there were trends toward improvement in immobility, visual impairment, and hearing impairment. Conclusions The risk-factor intervention strategy that we studied resulted in significant reductions in the number and duration of episodes of delirium in hospitalized older patients. The intervention had no significant effect on the severity of delirium or on recurrence rates; this finding suggests that primary prevention of delirium is probably the most effective treatment strategy. (N Engl J Med 1999;340:669-76.)

paragraphs.note: Abstract conclusion — the bundle reduced number and duration of delirium and primary prevention is the most effective strategy, supporting proactive application to every at-risk patient.

paragraphs.context: This controlled clinical trial provides evidence that a multicomponent, targeted intervention strategy, the Elder Life Program, is effective for the prevention of delirium in hospitalized older medical patients. The intervention prevented the initial development of delirium and reduced the total number of days of delirium. It was most effective in patients who were at intermediate risk for delirium at base line. Once an initial episode of delirium had occurred, however, the intervention had no significant effect on the severity of delirium or on the likelihood of recurrence. This finding has an important implication for the treatment of delirium: primary prevention is probably the most effective strategy. Once delirium has occurred, our intervention strategy will be less effective and less efficient.

claims.synthesis: All three sources agree that a multicomponent, risk-factor–targeted nonpharmacologic bundle reduces incident delirium in at-risk hospitalised non-ICU patients: the Cochrane 2016 review (RR 0.69, effect similar in medical and surgical settings) is the most directly on-scope source and governs the general step-down setting, underpinned by the Inouye 1999 HELP RCT (older medical patients) and the AGS 2015 strong recommendation (at-risk older surgical patients). paragraphs.context: Risk factors include non-modifiable conditions including advanced age, impaired pre-existing cognition, significant comorbidities, and potentially modifiable (precipitating) factors such as deep sedation, untreated trauma, pharmacological interactions, and new-onset infections [ 13 , 14 ]. Early recognition of POD features is key to delirium management, as there are several modifiable risk factors, such as new-onset infections, pain, inappropriate drug use and pharmacological interactions [ 13 , 14 ]. paragraphs.context: At presentation, assess people at risk for recent (within hours or days) changes or fluctuations that may indicate delirium.
paragraphs.highlight: At presentation, assess people at risk for recent (within hours or days) changes
paragraphs.note: Any recent change or fluctuation triggers a formal assessment — the trigger-on-change principle behind rescreening.

paragraphs.context: Ensure that any changes that may indicate delirium are documented in the person's record or notes. [2023]
paragraphs.highlight: documented in the person's record or notes
paragraphs.note: Supports the 'document it' step — record delirium-relevant findings in the notes; NICE frames this around documenting changes/indicators, which the tool extends to recording the screen result itself.

paragraphs.context: Be particularly vigilant for changes that may indicate hypoactive delirium, which are often missed, such as withdrawal, slow responses, reduced mobility and movement, worsened concentration and reduced appetite.
paragraphs.highlight: changes that may indicate hypoactive delirium, which are often missed
paragraphs.note: Nearest NICE match to the arousal warning, but about hypoactive delirium (reduced arousal/withdrawal) rather than normal arousal — a different, broader concept that must not be read as direct support for 'normal arousal does not exclude delirium'.

paragraphs.context: A person may already have delirium when they present to hospital or long-term care or it may develop during a hospital admission or residential stay in long-term care. Delirium can be hypoactive or hyperactive but some people show signs of both (mixed). People with hyperactive delirium have heightened arousal and can be restless, agitated and aggressive. People with hypoactive delirium become withdrawn, quiet and sleepy. Hypoactive and mixed delirium can be more difficult to recognise.
paragraphs.highlight: Hypoactive and mixed delirium can be more difficult to recognise
paragraphs.note: Definitional background — hypoactive/mixed delirium is harder to recognise — contextualizing why an unremarkable or negative screen must not be treated as ruling delirium out.

claims.synthesis: The two sources are complementary rather than conflicting: Beyer 2024 — validated in the intermediate/step-down care setting the tool targets — is the on-scope source for "normal arousal does not exclude delirium," because the CAM-IMC's point-based scoring makes the altered-arousal item non-mandatory so a fully alert (RASS 0) patient can still screen positive, while NICE CG103 governs "document it" and "rescreen with any change" through its daily-observation, assess-on-change and record-in-notes recommendations (for the broader hospital/long-term-care population). The nearest NICE match to the arousal point is its hypoactive-delirium vigilance guidance, which concerns reduced — not normal — arousal and should not be read as direct support for that clause.

claims.statement: Positive → find the cause (review meds first), manage without new harm, and hand the finding off.
claims.passage:
A high anticholinergic burden within 24 hours after admission was significantly associated with incident delirium. Although prospective studies need to confirm these results, discontinuing or substituting drugs with a score of ≥3 at admission might be a targeted intervention to reduce incident delirium.
Also Siddiqi 2016 (Cochrane) (p. 7): “We found multi-component interventions reduced the incidence of delirium compared to usual care (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.81; seven studies; 1950 participants; moderate-quality evidence).”
Supported. Review deliriogenic / anticholinergic medications (Lisibach 2022, p. 1; AGS 2015, p. 8); manage with the multicomponent bundle rather than antipsychotics (Siddiqi 2016, p. 7); hand off per NICE CG103 (not archived). A compressed restatement of the Act-on-a-positive card.
citations: Lisibach A, et al. Quantifying anticholinergic burden and its association with delirium (comparison of 19 scales). Br J Clin Pharmacol 2022;88:4915.
American Geriatrics Society. Abstracted clinical practice guideline for postoperative delirium in older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc 2015;63:142.
Siddiqi N, et al. Interventions for preventing delirium in hospitalised non-ICU patients. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;CD005563.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management in hospital and long-term care. CG103 (updated 2023).

perSource.label: NICE CG103
perSource.cite: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management in hospital and long-term care. CG103 (updated 2023).
perSource.note: Governing on-scope source: covers all three claim elements (find/manage the cause, review meds, manage without new harm, and document/hand off) for hospital and long-term care, including critical care.

paragraphs.context: In people diagnosed with delirium, identify and manage the possible underlying cause or combination of causes.
paragraphs.highlight: identify and manage the possible underlying
paragraphs.note: Recommendation 1.7.1 is the exact 'find the cause' step after a positive diagnosis — identify and manage the underlying cause or combination of causes.

paragraphs.context: Carry out a medication review for people taking multiple drugs, taking into account both the type and number of medications. For information on medicines optimisation see the NICE guideline on medicines optimisation. [2010]
paragraphs.highlight: Carry out a medication review for people taking multiple drugs, taking into account both the type and number of medications
paragraphs.note: Direct support for 'review meds first'; NICE lists medication review among its measures for people taking multiple drugs (recommendation 1.4.10).

paragraphs.context: others, first use verbal and non-verbal techniques to de-escalate the situation.
paragraphs.highlight: first use verbal and non-verbal techniques to de-escalate the situation
paragraphs.note: Recommendation 1.7.3 — non-pharmacological de-escalation first for a distressed patient, the 'manage without new harm' approach.

paragraphs.context: inappropriate, consider giving short-term haloperidol (usually for 1 week or less).
paragraphs.highlight: consider giving short-term haloperidol (usually for 1 week or less)
paragraphs.note: Recommendation 1.7.4 — only if de-escalation fails, cautious short-term low-dose haloperidol with MHRA risk caveats: the drug-use guardrail against new harm.

paragraphs.context: Ensure that the diagnosis of delirium is documented both in the person's record or notes, and in their primary care health record.
paragraphs.highlight: the diagnosis of delirium is documented both in the person's record
paragraphs.note: Recommendation 1.6.4 supports 'hand the finding off' — document the diagnosis in the person's notes and their primary care health record.

perSource.label: AGS 2015 (postoperative delirium guideline)
perSource.cite: American Geriatrics Society. Abstracted clinical practice guideline for postoperative delirium in older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc 2015;63:142.
perSource.note: Strongly supports the identify-and-manage-cause, review/avoid-harmful-medication, and avoid-harmful-sedation/restraint elements; population is postoperative older surgical adults and it does not address the hand-off.

paragraphs.context: Recommendation--The healthcare professional should perform a medical evaluation, make medication and/or environmental adjustments, and order appropriate diagnostic tests and clinical consultations after an older adult has been diagnosed with postoperative delirium to identify and manage underlying contributors to delirium (strength of recommendation: strong; quality of evidence: low).
paragraphs.highlight: make medication and/or environmental adjustments, and order appropriate diagnostic tests and clinical consultations
paragraphs.note: Recommendation IV 'Identify and Manage Causes of Delirium' is the exact find-the-cause / adjust-medications workflow after diagnosis; population is postoperative older adults.

paragraphs.context: The healthcare professional should perform a medical evaluation, make medication and/or environmental adjustments, and order appropriate diagnostic tests and clinical consultations after an older adult has been diagnosed with postoperative delirium to identify and manage underlying contributors to delirium
paragraphs.highlight: identify and manage underlying contributors to delirium
paragraphs.note: Section IV recommendation: on a positive finding, evaluate, adjust medications/environment, and order tests/consultations to find and manage the cause.

paragraphs.context: A. Evidence for Recommendation: Relevant medications or medication classes include benzodiazepines, anticholinergics (e.g., cyclobenzaprine, oxybutynin, prochlorperazine, promethazine, tricyclic antidepressants, paroxetine and drugs with high anticholinergic properties), diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, histamine2-receptor antagonists (e.g., cimetidine), sedative-hypnotics, and meperidine. Since the studies regarding specific medications provide generally low-level evidence, the current recommendation relied on the 2012 AGS Beers Criteria.11 Current evidence most strongly associates use of anticholinergic drugs, meperidine and benzodiazepines with increased postoperative delirium. Studies have identified the following medications with increased delirium: diphenhydramine,63ET meperidine,2ET midazolam,64ET and anticholinergic medications.65ET Drugs that contribute to serotonin syndrome can increase delirium risk, as can the use of multiple medications (five or greater).
paragraphs.highlight: Current evidence most strongly associates use of anticholinergic drugs, meperidine and benzodiazepines with increased postoperative delirium
paragraphs.note: Names the drug classes to target when reviewing meds (anticholinergics, meperidine, benzodiazepines) — supports 'review meds first'; postoperative population.

paragraphs.context: Recommendation--The prescribing practitioner should not prescribe antipsychotic or benzodiazepine medications for the treatment of older adults with postoperative delirium who are not agitated and threatening substantial harm to self or others (strength of recommendation: strong; quality of evidence: low).
paragraphs.highlight: should not prescribe antipsychotic or benzodiazepine medications for the treatment of older adults with postoperative delirium who are not agitated
paragraphs.note: Recommendation XIV supports 'manage without new harm' — do not reach for antipsychotics/benzodiazepines in non-agitated delirium.

paragraphs.context: B. Potential Harms of Recommendation: This recommendation balances the risks of delay in treatment for underlying cause(s) of delirium with the risks and costs of diagnostic tests and procedures, as well as the possibility of pain and infection. Overuse of neuroimaging (computed tomography (CT)/magnet resonance imaging (MRI)) is an additional potential risk. For agitated patients, sedation and/or restraints may be required to obtain these studies; however, both sedating medications and restraints may exacerbate delirium. The AGS recommends avoiding physical restraints to manage behavioral symptoms of hospitalized older adults with delirium.46 See complete harms statement in the AGS Delirium Guideline at .
paragraphs.highlight: both sedating medications and restraints may exacerbate delirium
paragraphs.note: Harms statement for Recommendation IV — sedating drugs and restraints can worsen delirium; the 'without new harm' guardrail.

perSource.label: Lisibach 2022 (anticholinergic burden)
perSource.cite: Lisibach A, et al. Quantifying anticholinergic burden and its association with delirium (comparison of 19 scales). Br J Clin Pharmacol 2022;88:4915.
perSource.note: Substantiates the 'review meds first' element specifically for anticholinergic burden in non-ICU older inpatients; frames deprescribing as reducing incident delirium and does not address the other claim elements.

paragraphs.context: Although prospective studies need to confirm these results, discontinuing or substituting drugs with a score of 3 at admission might be a targeted intervention to reduce incident delirium.
paragraphs.highlight: discontinuing or substituting drugs with a score of 3 at admission might be a targeted intervention to reduce incident delirium
paragraphs.note: Supports 'review meds first' — discontinuing/substituting high-anticholinergic drugs is a targeted intervention to reduce delirium; population is non-ICU older inpatients (ICU stays >24h excluded).

paragraphs.context: A cumulative ACH burden score of three points or more can be considered a high burden, which was statistically significantly and independently associated with the development of delirium during hospitalisation. The ABSs are convenient clinical tools to measure the ACH burden in hospitalised patients. Newer high‐quality ABSs built from previously published scales seem to perform better. However, cut‐off values might differ depending on the scale and outcome studied. Discontinuing or substituting drugs with an ACH score of three points or more upon admission might be a targeted intervention to reduce the risk of delirium development. However, it should be noted that delirium is a multifactorial syndrome, and that drugs are only one factor to be considered in delirium prevention. Further studies should be conducted in order to prospectively verify whether discontinuing drugs with ACH properties might reduce delirium occurrences.
paragraphs.highlight: drugs are only one factor to be considered in delirium prevention
paragraphs.note: Reinforces reviewing meds while cautioning that delirium is multifactorial and drugs are only one contributor — supports 'find the cause' without overclaiming meds as the sole cause.

paragraphs.context: A cumulative anticholinergic burden score of 3 points within the first 24 hours of admission is associated with delirium development during hospitalisation.
paragraphs.highlight: A cumulative anticholinergic burden score of 3 points within the first 24 hours of admission is associated with delirium development during hospitalisation
paragraphs.note: The specific anticholinergic-burden-to-delirium association underpinning the review-meds action; narrower than the general 'review meds first' step.

perSource.label: Siddiqi 2016 (Cochrane)
perSource.cite: Siddiqi N, et al. Interventions for preventing delirium in hospitalised non-ICU patients. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;CD005563.
perSource.note: Nearest match on multi-component and medication approaches but scoped to PREVENTION of delirium in hospitalised non-ICU patients, not acting on a positive screen — a different-intervention scope that does not govern this claim.

paragraphs.context: There is strong evidence supporting multi-component interventions to prevent delirium in hospitalised patients. There is no clear evidence that cholinesterase inhibitors, antipsychotic medication or melatonin reduce the incidence of delirium. Using the Bispectral Index to monitor and control depth of anaesthesia reduces the incidence of postoperative delirium. The role of drugs and other anaesthetic techniques to prevent delirium remains uncertain.
paragraphs.highlight: There is no clear evidence that cholinesterase inhibitors, antipsychotic medication or melatonin reduce the incidence of delirium
paragraphs.note: Authors' conclusion is about PREVENTING delirium before onset, not the post-positive management workflow — shares keywords (medications, multi-component) but a different intervention target.

paragraphs.context: There is moderate-quality evidence to indicate that multi-component interventions reduce the incidence of delirium. The evidence supports implementing multi-component delirium prevention interventions into routine care for patients in hospital.
paragraphs.highlight: implementing multi-component delirium prevention interventions into routine care for patients in hospital
paragraphs.note: Recommends multi-component PREVENTION into routine care, not acting on an established positive screen.

paragraphs.context: There are many risk factors for developing delirium (e.g. infection, dehydration, certain medications). Therefore, one approach (called `multi-component interventions') to preventing delirium is to target these multiple risk factors. Some medications have e ects on the brain chemicals implicated in developing delirium, and may, therefore, have a role in prevention. There are also a number of other interventions that target delirium risk factors related to anaesthesia and medical treatment around the time of surgery.
paragraphs.highlight: many risk factors for developing delirium (e.g. infection, dehydration, certain medications)
paragraphs.note: Background that medications are among delirium risk factors — supports the rationale for reviewing meds, but framed for prevention.

claims.synthesis: The on-scope guidance agrees on the workflow. NICE CG103 governs this "act on a positive" step: identify and manage the underlying cause(s) (including medication review), de-escalate non-pharmacologically first with only cautious short-term haloperidol if needed, and document the diagnosis in the person's notes and primary-care record (the hand-off). AGS 2015 concurs on identifying/managing the cause and avoiding harmful sedatives, restraints and non-indicated antipsychotics/benzodiazepines, though its population is postoperative older adults; Lisibach 2022 supports "review meds first" specifically for anticholinergic burden in non-ICU older inpatients (narrower). Siddiqi 2016 is the nearest match on multi-component/medication approaches but addresses prevention rather than acting on a positive screen — a different-intervention scope, so it does not govern this claim.

claims.statement: RASS −4/−5 — stupor or coma. Record it, and reassess when the patient responds to voice.
claims.passage:
for diagnosing POD in intubated patients cannot make use of the feature ‘disorientation’, as this requires verbal communication. Other tools such as the 4AT test for disorientation but are not established in ICU settings.
Same content as the arousal-gate stop (indirect / standard RASS practice) — see stage 2.
citations: Beyer LP, et al. Disorientation as a delirium feature in non-intubated patients: development and evaluation of the CAM-IMC. BMC Anesthesiol 2024;24:451.
Sessler CN, et al. The Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale: validity and reliability in adult ICU patients. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2002;166:1338.

perSource.label: Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC)
perSource.cite: Beyer LP, et al. Disorientation as a delirium feature in non-intubated patients: development and evaluation of the CAM-IMC. BMC Anesthesiol 2024;24:451.
perSource.note: CAM-IMC validation in non-intubated cardiac-surgery step-down patients; corroborates that the setting uses RASS/level-of-consciousness and defines RASS -5 as deeply sedated, but never states the RASS -4/-5 unable-to-assess record-and-reassess-on-voice gate.

paragraphs.context: RASS ranges from -5 (deeply sedated) to +4 (aggressive)
paragraphs.highlight: -5 (deeply sedated)
paragraphs.note: Table 1 footnote defining the RASS scale endpoints (RASS -5 = deeply sedated, the stupor/coma end); corroborates the definitional half of the claim but not the record-and-reassess gating action.

paragraphs.context: Background Disorientation is an early indicator of developing postoperative delirium (POD), which is associated with increased mortality and cognitive decline. The well-established "Confusion-Assessment-Method-for-IntensiveCare-Unit" (CAM-ICU) for diagnosing POD in intubated patients cannot make use of the feature `disorientation', as this requires verbal communication. Other tools such as the 4AT test for disorientation but are not established in ICU settings. We therefore combined test-variables of the CAM-ICU (level of consciousness, fluctuating mental status and inattention) with verbal testing for disorientation to develop and enhance diagnostic accuracy of the "Confusion Assessment Method for Intermediate Care Unit" (CAM-IMC). In the present study we describe the development and the evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy of the CAM-IMC.
paragraphs.highlight: level of consciousness, fluctuating mental status and inattention
paragraphs.note: Establishes that the step-down CAM-IMC tool incorporates the CAM-ICU level-of-consciousness/RASS variable and requires verbal communication, setting the scene for an arousal gate but not stating the RASS -4/-5 defer rule.

paragraphs.context: Among 178 scheduled cardiac surgery patients, 155 proved eligible between November 2021 and February 2022, 23 of which were excluded. In these, 624 paired examinations were completed on the first three postoperative days (see flowchart in Fig. 2 ). Aggressive patients could not be accurately examined due to lack of cooperation and no plausible disorientation assessment.
paragraphs.highlight: Aggressive patients could not be accurately examined
paragraphs.note: An unable-to-assess scenario at the opposite, agitated (RASS-positive) end of the arousal spectrum from the claim's RASS -4/-5 stupor/coma; shares the unable-to-examine keyword but must not be read as supporting the coma/sedation defer rule.

paragraphs.context: This cohort study evaluates the test performance of the newly developed CAM-IMC and its disorientation component in a prospective cohort study. The CAM-IMC shows a sensitivity of 0.96 and specificity of 0.94 in diagnosis of POD in non-intubated postoperative cardiac surgery patients. Its test performance is comparable to the widely used CAM-ICU demonstrating a high level of accuracy [ 19 ]. While testing for disorientation alone shows good test performance values, it does not surpass the CAM-IMC. The study indicates that using the CAM-IMC by combing the features of the CAM-ICU with assessing of disorientation as a verbal testing variable, improves effectiveness and provides excellent sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing POD. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating verbal testing for disorientation whenever patients are accessible to oral evaluation to improve POD diagnostics. The CAM-IMC outperforms each individual feature of the CAM-IMC.
paragraphs.highlight: whenever patients are accessible to oral evaluation
paragraphs.note: Conditions verbal disorientation testing on the patient being accessible to oral evaluation - conceptually adjacent to the unable-to-assess gate but framed around verbal-test accessibility, not the RASS -4/-5 record-and-reassess-when-responds-to-voice rule.

perSource.label: Sessler 2002 (RASS)
perSource.cite: Sessler CN, et al. The Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale: validity and reliability in adult ICU patients. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2002;166:1338.
perSource.note: The RASS validation reference; contributes the scale's arousal anchor points that govern the gate - RASS -4 (no response to voice, movement to physical stimulation) and RASS -5 (unarousable, no response to voice or physical stimulation) - and the 'responds to voice' threshold for resuming assessment. Cited by the 'Loop - unable to assess' section; per-instruction web source, so no paragraph extraction.

claims.synthesis: Neither cited source states the claim's gating rule verbatim: the direct authority for the RASS -4/-5 arousal threshold (stupor/coma, unarousable) and the "responds to voice" cue for resuming assessment is Sessler 2002 (RASS), the web source, which governs here. Beyer 2024 (the CAM-IMC step-down validation named as primary anchor) only corroborates that the setting uses RASS/level-of-consciousness and defines RASS -5 as deeply sedated; its keyword-adjacent passages - aggressive patients who could not be examined, and verbal testing only when patients are accessible to oral evaluation - are different-scope and must not be read as direct support.

claims.statement: On transfer / hand-off of a positive screen: (1) screen used and result (CAM-IMC score / band); (2) suspected cause(s) and what was ruled out; (3) interventions started (bundle, medication changes); (4) reassessment / follow-up plan for the receiving team.

legend: deliriumtool.com/templates · prepared July 31, 2026; adult step-down / progressive-care tool added August 1, 2026

This workbook lists every clinical statement that can appear on the printable bedside templates, together with the published source each statement cites and the passage from that source that supports it. For sources held in the reference archive, the supporting passage is shown in its surrounding paragraph with the exact cited text in bold blue; the line above each passage gives the source and page (and the paragraph number where the source's layout allows one to be counted). Passages were checked against the archive copy. Rows where the cited source does not state the claim are shaded red for review.

Each template has its own sheet, one row per printed statement. Column filters are enabled. The Reviewer decision and Notes columns are reserved for the review team; the decision column offers Accept, Revise wording, Remove, Needs source, and Check evidence. The All references sheet lists each source once, with the sections that rely on it, for source-level sign-off.
Cited clinical content — screening logic, thresholds, prevention-bundle items, and medication cautions drawn from published guidelines and validated instruments.
Validated instrument wording — the screening tools themselves (CAM-ICU, RASS, CAPD, DTS, bCAM, 4AT). This wording is reproduced from the instrument and is not editable by sites.
Local protocol — the nurse care pathway and any site-authored sections. Sites adapt these to their own practice; they carry no central citation and need no reference review.
Full text, p. N — the quoted passage appears in the source at the page shown.
Abstract / Web page — the source is quoted from its public abstract or web page rather than an archive copy.
Source not accessible — the source could not be consulted directly; verify against the DOI given in the row.
Not stated in cited source — no supporting statement was found in the source(s) the row cites. Review these rows first; several are general-practice items whose support lies outside the cited papers.

Coverage: 241 printed statements in total across eight templates. 216 cite central sources; 25 are site-customized rows with no citation to review. Of the 216, 169 are supported by a full-text passage (168 page-confirmed), 24 by an abstract or web source, 18 are flagged where the cited source does not state the claim, and 5 (all on the step-down templates) cite a guideline or instrument whose wording is held outside the local archive — NICE CG103 and the Sessler/Ely RASS anchor set. The 37 step-down statements are all sourced: 32 are anchored to a verbatim full-text passage and none are flagged.

Every source was checked against its indexed record (CrossRef or PubMed) or the issuing organization’s site. All 70 source rows are real publications or guidelines; none are fabricated. In the original set, two corrections were identified and are noted in the Citation check column of the All references sheet: the Hayhurst 2020 author list is cited incorrectly, and Project BETA belongs to the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry rather than the APA. The 16 step-down sources were re-checked online: 15 of 16 identifiers resolve with matching author, year, and title; the sixteenth (AGS 2015 postoperative-delirium guideline, doi 10.1111/jgs.13281) resolves to the correct title but CrossRef lists its 2014 online-first date rather than the 2015 print issue (J Am Geriatr Soc 2015;63:142). NICE CG103 carries no DOI/PMID and is the issuing body’s record.

**Two-step DTS → bCAM (Han 2013; Vanderbilt DTS/bCAM manuals v1.0; Geriatric

The step-down tool screens the verbal, monitored-but-non-intubated
(intermediate-care / progressive-care) patient, where the CAM-ICU loses
sensitivity for the mild and hypoactive delirium common on the ward. It
implements the CAM-IMC as the screen, a RASS arousal gate, the Martinez

The setting sits between the ICU tool (CAM-ICU) and a general acute ward, where
the ward-validated 3D-CAM or the 4AT apply (Marcantonio 2014; SIGN 157; NICE
CG103); the Setup tab carries that routing.
A weighted, additive 0–10 screen, positive at ≥ 3 —
the Youden-index cut-off in the validation cohort — developed and validated in
non-intubated postoperative cardiac-surgery patients in an intermediate-care
unit (sensitivity 0.96, specificity 0.94). Four elements score into the total:
acute change or fluctuating course (dichotomous, +1) and altered level of
consciousness (dichotomous, RASS ≠ 0 → +1); inattention (0–3), read as the
ten-letter word "ANANASBAUM" or "CASABLANCA" with a hand squeeze on each "A"
(one point per error, the item positive at ≥ 3 errors); and disorientation
(0–5) across five dimensions — age, date of birth, place, year, and situational
awareness — one point per error, the item positive at ≥ 2 errors. Unlike the
CAM-ICU, the point system does not gate on a positive acute-change feature:
disorientation or inattention can each drive a positive result on their own.

Of 103 agents, the strongest classes (benzodiazepines, opioids, anticholinergics) are on by default and the rest are opt-in; benzodiazepines, strong anticholinergics, and meperidine carry a citation-backed

Antipsychotics have not been shown to treat or shorten delirium (MIND-USA negative; PADIS 2025 was unable to recommend for or against); the tool restricts them to short-term control of dangerous agitation with documented indication, QTc monitoring, daily reassessment, and no discharge continuation without a psychiatric indication. It is a maintenance and provenance record for the code in this repository, not a clinical endorsement. Clinical governance for any deployment is the adopter's responsibility (§6.1).

Anyone who deploys this tool, or a derivative of it, for clinical use owns the clinical governance for that deployment: validating the content against current sources for their population, obtaining whatever local clinical, pharmacy, and information-governance review or sign-off their institution requires, and making their own regulatory determination for their jurisdiction and intended use. 7.1 Screening: arousal gate + CAPD / pCAM-ICU / psCAM-ICU
The user picks the validated screen for the child's age and developmental level; arousal is scored first as the gate.

CAPD (Cornell Assessment of Pediatric Delirium), all ages (0–21 yr).

Eight-item observational nursing screen rated over the shift against age-expected behavior; each item 0–4 (total 0–32). Items 1–4 (eye contact, purposeful actions, awareness, communication) are reverse-scored (Never = 4 … Always = 0); items 5–8 (restless, inconsolable, underactive, slow to respond) are scored Never = 0 … Always = 4.
Developmental-delay caveat surfaced at the result

(matching in-app text): CAPD ≥ 9 remains positive, but specificity falls in baseline developmental delay (Traube 2014: 51.2% at ≥ 9; Gupta 2021: 44.8% overall, 16.5% with delay in ventilated children), so the result is interpreted against the child's own developmental baseline and the anchors, with experienced-clinician or pediatric-psychiatry review when needed. The tool does not advise substituting a higher cut point: reduced specificity is a false-positive problem, not a validated replacement threshold, and the ventilated-cohort ≥ 17 figure is population-specific. The 0–32 score and positive/negative are withheld until all eight items are rated.

the source anchor table defines point-age columns (NB, 4 wk, 6 wk, 8 wk, 28 wk, 1 yr, 2 yr); the tool maps a developmental age to the column whose labeled age it has reached (cuts at ≈0.92 / 1.38 / 1.84 / 6.44 / 12 / 24 months), so a child at or past a labeled age sees that column's anchors. The previously listed "~0.015–0.15 mg/kg/dose IV q6–8h" was the observed per-dose range of a single 5-patient 2002 case series (Harrison, via Capino 2020 Table 1, ventilated children on neuromuscular blockade) that Capino itself declines to convert into a recommendation; at q6h its upper bound permits 0.60 mg/kg/day, several-fold above published institutional protocols (e.g. maintenance 0.015–0.025 mg/kg/dose q6h with a 0.45 mg/kg/day maximum, or daily-dose titration 0.05 → 0.15 mg/kg/day divided for infants and young children). Baseline 12-lead ECG (QTc), electrolytes, QT-drug review; read the QTc against age-, sex-, rhythm- and correction-formula-appropriate limits. (The earlier "> 450–500 ms or ≥ 25% rise" was ambiguous, and the 25% delta is unsupported in the cited pediatric sources and behaves unintuitively: 25% of a 400 ms baseline is 100 ms, missing a clinically meaningful 60 ms change.) A borderline/prolonged result prompts repeat/verify ECG, electrolyte correction, and interacting-drug review; QTc ≥ 500 ms or a substantial absolute rise (commonly ≥ 60 ms in QT-safety practice) warrants urgent prescriber/pharmacy review under the local cardiology or medication-safety protocol, which sets the stop/reduce thresholds. Watch EPS/dystonia (most with haloperidol), NMS, and metabolic effects (olanzapine/quetiapine highest).
